Perspectives Theorem 10.2.1 is due to Lemaire [287] and Sacks and Uhlenbeck [367].
Theorem 10.2.5 is again due to Sacks and Uhlenbeck [367]. In particular, Sacks and Uhlenbeck
had discovered the important phenomenon of bubbling of minimal 2-spheres. (In the context of
surfaces of constant mean curvature, a bubbling phenomenon was independently discovered by
Wente [429].)
    Other approaches to these results were found by Struwe [400], Chang [68] and Jost, see [227].
A detailed proof of Theorem 10.2.1 is given in [245].
10.2 The Existence of Harmonic Maps in Two Dimensions                                             611


   The method of M. Struwe and K.C. Chang consists in studying the associated parabolic
problem. Thus, given ' W † ! N; one studies solutions of

                                    f W †  Œ0; 1/ ! N;
                                             f .z; 0/ D '. /;
                                           @f
                                              .z; t/ D . f .z; t//;
                                           @t
where the tension field is computed w.r.t. the z variable. One can then show that a solution can
develop at most finitely many singularities. These singularities correspond to the splitting off of
minimal 2-spheres. In the limit t ! 1, one obtains a harmonic map f .
    The construction presented in this section is refined in [227]. There, also various existence
results for unstable harmonic maps are presented. Any type of critical point theory, e.g. Morse
theory, for harmonic maps in two dimensions has to take the splitting off of minimal 2-spheres into
account. In certain instances, however, one may show that this phenomenon can be excluded. A
prototype of such a result is the following
Theorem Let † be a compact Riemann surface with boundary, N a Riemannian manifold
diffeomorphic to S2 (thus, the condition 2 .N/ D 0 is not satisfied). Let g W @† ! N nonconstant.
Then there exist at least two harmonic maps f1 ; f2 W † ! N with fij@† D g.
    This result is due to Brézis and Coron [57] and Jost [224]. In order to prove this theorem, one
first minimizes the energy over all maps f W † ! N with fj@† D g and obtains a harmonic u (see
the remark after Theorem 10.2.3). By careful comparison constructions one then exhibits another
homotopy class ˛ of maps from † to N (not containing u/ with

                              inffE. f / W f 2 ˛g < E.u/ C Area .N/:

One then shows that if minimizing energy in some homotopy class leads to the splitting off of a
minimal 2-sphere, the energy would be lowered by an amount of at least the energy of that minimal
sphere. Since N is diffeomorphic to S2 , the energy of such a minimal sphere would be at least the
area of N. Since, however, u realizes the absolute minimum of energy among all maps with the
prescribed boundary values, the above inequality excludes the splitting off of a minimal 2-sphere
during the minimization of the energy in the class ˛.
    We have described the preceding argument in some detail because it forms a paradigm for other
conformally invariant variational problems (Yang–Mills equations in four dimensions, constant
mean curvature surfaces, Yamabe problem, etc.). Some further discussion of such limit cases of
the Palais–Smale condition may be found in [402] and in the references given there.
    Returning to the critical point theory for two-dimensional harmonic maps, we also mention
Ding [108] and the survey article [228] where many further references can be found.
    The bubbling phenomenon exhibited in Theorems 10.2.4 and 10.2.5 pertains to J-holomorphic
curves, and it has been analyzed in detail by Parker-Wolfson [342] and Ye [449]. This is quite
important in the context of Gromov’s applications of J-holomorphic curves in symplectic topology,
see [304].
    In this context, we should also discuss the Plateau problem for minimal surfaces. In its simplest
form, we consider a smooth (or, more generally, a rectifiable) closed Jordan curve  in R3 and
seek a minimal surface with boundary . In the parametric version of the problem, we look for
a harmonic and conformal f W D ! R3 (D D unit disk) mapping @D monotonically onto 
(a monotonic map between curves is defined to be a uniform limit of homeomorphisms). In this
form, the problem was solved by J. Douglas [117, 118, 120] and T. Radó [354, 355]. The problem
was then extended by Douglas to configurations of more than one disjoint curves 1 ; : : : ; k and/or
minimal surfaces of other topological type [119, 121]. He found a condition [122, 123] (the so-
called Douglas condition) guaranteeing the existence of minimal surfaces of some prescribed
topological type. Since at that time, however, the degeneration of conformal structures of Riemann
surfaces was not yet well enough understood, in the competing work of Douglas [122–124] and
612                                                    10 Harmonic Maps from Riemann Surfaces


Courant [96, 97], no general proof of the sufficiency of Douglas’ criterion for the existence of
higher genus minimal surfaces was achieved. The first complete proof was obtained in [225];
in fact, that proof not only works in Euclidean space, but also in Riemannian manifolds. It was
also asked whether one may find unstable minimal surfaces with prescribed boundary. These
questions were investigated by Courant [98] and Shiffman [388, 389]. Struwe [399, 401] introduced
a functional analytical approach and developed a Morse theory for minimal surfaces of disk
and annulus type The most comprehensive critical point theory for minimal surfaces in R3 was
developed in Jost and Struwe [254] where also references to earlier contributions are given. In some
sense, this work combines the approaches of [225] and [399, 401]. The approach was developed
further in [232] where it was shown that a configuration of two linked circles bounds infinitely
many (non-orientable) minimal surfaces. Earlier, Morgan [320] had constructed a configuration of
four circles in three parallel planes with their centers on the same line that bounds infinitely many
minimal surfaces, in fact even a continuum of minimal surfaces. Gulliver and Hildebrandt [190]
had then shown that a configuration of three circles in three parallel planes with their centers on the
same line can also bound a continuum of minimal surfaces. While the example in [232] consists of
only two curves, it is still an open question whether a single smooth Jordan curve in R3 can bound
infinitely many minimal surfaces. In contrast to such multiplicity results, a minimal disk with a
smooth Plateau boundary curve is unique when the total curvature of that curve is  4, as shown
by Nitsche [337] for < 4 and by Li-Jost [293] in general.
    The Plateau problem in Riemannian manifolds (instead of just R3 ) was solved by C. Morrey
[324], and as mentioned, the higher genus case was treated in [225]. Results pointing into the
direction of a general Morse theory for minimal surfaces in Riemannian manifolds may be found
in Jost [227].
    There also exists the geometric measure theory approach to minimal surfaces. Here, one tries
to represent a minimal surface not as the image of a map of a Riemann surface, but directly as
a submanifold of the given ambient space. In the parametric approach, one had to generalize
the space of smooth maps to a Sobolev space, in order to guarantee the existence of limits of
minimizing sequences. For the same reason, in the measure theoretic approach, the space of
submanifolds has to be generalized to the one of currents. A submanifold of dimension k yields a
linear functional on the space of differential forms of degree k by integration, and so the space of
k-currents is defined as a space dual to the one of k-forms. One may then minimize a generalized
version of area, the so-called mass, on the space of currents. This approach is valid in any
dimension and codimension, in contrast to the parametric one that is restricted to 2 dimensions.
If the codimension is 1 and the dimension at most 7, then such a mass minimizing current is
regular in the sense that it represents a smooth submanifold. Otherwise, singularities may occur.
In particular, any smooth Jordan curve in R3 bounds an embedded minimal surface, see Hardt
and Simon [198]. For a general treatment of the concepts and the approach of geometric measure
theory, we recommend Federer [140] and Almgren [7].
    Minimal surfaces in Riemannian manifolds have found important geometric applications. Let
us mention a few selected ones.
    In the proof of the Bonnet–Myers theorem (Corollary 6.3.1), we have seen how information
about geodesics and their stability can be used to reach topological consequences for manifolds of
positive Ricci curvature. This suggests that information about the stability of minimal surfaces
may likewise be used to obtain restrictions on the topology of positively curved manifolds.
The first instance of an important application of minimal 2-spheres in the presence of positive
curvature is Siu and Yau [393]. Micallef and Moore [307] showed that minimal 2-spheres can
be used to prove that any compact Riemannian manifold with positive curvature operator (i.e.
R.; / D 2 .M/ ! 2 .M/ is a positive operator; this in particular implies positive sectional
curvature) is diffeomorphic to a sphere. Also, the sphere theorem (see Short survey on curvature
and topology, above) was proved under the assumption of pointwise pinching only (i.e. at each
point, the maximal ratio between sectional curvatures is less than 4).
    There are also important applications of minimal surfaces in three-dimensional topology. The
so-called Dehn lemma, whose first complete proof was given by Papkyriakopoulos, asserts that
if S is a differentiably embedded surface in a compact differentiable three-manifold M and if 
10.3 Regularity Results                                                                      613


is an embedded curve on S that is homotopically trivial in M (i.e. Œ D 0 2 1 .M// then 
bounds an embedded disk. Meeks and Yau [306] showed that in this case, if we equip M with a
Riemannian metric in such a way that S is convex, the solution of the parametric Plateau problem
with boundary  is embedded. Thus, one obtains an embedded minimal disk bounded by . Tomi
and Tromba [419] had shown earlier that an extreme curve, that is, a curve on the boundary of a
convex body in R3 , bounds an embedded minimal disk, and Almgren and Simon [8] had shown
that such an embedded minimal disk can be obtained by minimizing the area among all embedded
disks. The proof of Tomi and Tromba uses a degree argument, whereas Almgren and Simon employ
tools from geometric measure theory. The proof of Meeks and Yau shows that the area-minimizing
disk is embedded and utilizes some constructions from three-dimensional topology. The work of
Meeks and Yau represents an analytical proof of Dehn’s lemma. The important fact is that they
have found a canonical solution of the problem. Assume for example that some compact group G
acts on M, leaving  invariant. One may then average the metric of M under the action of G and
obtain a new Riemannian metric on M for which G acts by isometries. Since  is G-invariant, one
may then also find a G-invariant minimal disk bounded by . If one chooses this disk to be area
minimizing in its class, one may then show again that it is embedded. This equivariant version of
Dehn’s lemma of Meeks–Yau then has applications to the classification of discrete group actions
on 3-manifolds, see [24].




10.3 Regularity Results

geometric analysis in contrast to standard PDE theory is that regularity is a global
question in the target). Thus, we consider regularity questions for harmonic maps
from Riemann surfaces locally and assume that the domain is the unit disk D. Since
we shall see that the regularity question for harmonic maps on Riemann surfaces
can essentially be reduced to the consideration of isolated singularities, we shall
also use the punctured unit disk

Perspectives The regularity theory for non-linear two-dimensional geometric variational prob-
lems began with Hildebrandt’s proof of the smoothness at a Plateau boundary for minimal surfaces
[208]. An account of the development of such regularity theory can be found in [227], where many
further references are given.
    In Theorem 10.3.2, we have shown that weakly harmonic and conformal maps of finite energy
from a Riemann surface into a Riemannian manifold (of bounded geometry) are continuous. The
conformality of the map is not needed for this regularity result as was shown by Hélein [205].
A systematic treatment is given in [206]. The removability of isolated singularities of weakly
harmonic maps was obtained by Sacks and Uhlenbeck [367]. The proof of the continuity of weak
minimal surfaces given here partly uses some arguments of Grüter [188]. A very powerful new
approach to the regularity theory of harmonic map type variational problems was developed by
Rivière [362] and Rivière-Struwe [363].




Basic Exercises for Chap. 10

1. The 2-sphere: Consider a complex polynomial p.z/ D ak zk C ak1 zk1 : : : a0
   of degree k (ak ¤ 0) in the complex plane C. Show that this induces (via
   stereographic projection) a holomorphic map S2 ! S2 of degree k (i.e., a generic
   point in S2 has k preimages).
10.3 Regularity Results                                                          629


2. 2-tori:
   (a) Show that every two-dimensional torus carries the structure of a Riemann
       surface. (Hint: Take the complex structure induced by that of C.)
   (b) Although by the preceding exercise, every two-dimensional torus carries a
       complex structure, not every harmonic map between two-dimensional tori is
       holomorphic.
   (c) Determine all holomorphic quadratic differentials on a two-dimensional
       torus, and all holomorphic quadratic differentials on an annular region fz 2
       C W r1  jzj  r2 g .0 < r1 < r2 / that are real on the boundary.

   Corollary 11.1.1 constitutes another instance of the phenomenon of selfduality
that we already encountered in §4.2 when we discussed the Yang–Mills functional
on a four-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Equations (11.1.30), (11.1.31) are also
called selfduality equations because the solutions of these first order equations are
precisely those solutions of (11.1.6), (11.1.7) that realize the lower bound imposed
by the topology for the functional and, if they exist, yield the absolute minima for
the functional considered. In fact, this remark, namely that these equations hold
for the absolute minima, makes it clear that any solution of (11.1.30), (11.1.31)
automatically also solves (11.1.6), (11.1.7), as the latter are the Euler–Lagrange
equations for the Ginzburg–Landau functional, and as such have to be satisfied in
particular by minimizers of that functional. Of course, it may also be checked by a
direct computation that solutions of (11.1.30), (11.1.31) also solve (11.1.6), (11.1.7).

Perspectives It was shown by Taubes [407] that on R2 , one may solve the Ginzburg–
Landau equations with any given finite collection prescribed as zero set for ', with prescribed
multiplicities. This result was extended to compact Riemann surfaces by Bradlow and García-
Prada, and these authors also found generalizations on higher dimensional Kähler manifolds.
References include [48, 49, 160–162]. We should also mention Hitchin’s penetrating study [212]
of the equations

                                                  @A ' D 0;
                                         FA C Œ'; '  D 0

on a compact Riemann surface.
    The limit analysis for  ! 0 of the functional L .'; A/ and the solutions of
Eqs. (11.1.35), (11.1.36) on a compact Riemann surface has been carried out by Hong, Jost
and Struwe [216]. The result is that away from the prescribed zero set of ' (the “vortices”), j' j
uniformly converges to 1, and DA ' and dA uniformly converge to 0, whereas the curvature in
the limit becomes a sum of delta distributions concentrated at the vortices. Of course, the number
of vortices counted with multiplicity has to equal the degree of the line bundle L, deg L. This result
thus yields a method for degenerating a line bundle on a Riemann surface into a flat line bundle
with deg L singular points (counted with multiplicity) and a covariantly constant section.
    Results for the ' 6 theory on a compact torus can be found in Caffarelli and Yang [62], Tarantello
[406], Ding, Jost, Li and Wang [110]. For the case of S2 , see Ding, Jost, Li and Wang [111]. The
general case was solved by Ding, Jost, Li, Peng and Wang [109].

Perspectives The Seiberg–Witten equations were introduced by Seiberg and Witten [385, 386].
The mathematical relevance of these equations was first shown by Witten [437], Taubes [409, 410],
Kronheimer and Mrowka [281]. Further references can be found in the monographs of Salamon
[369] and Morgan [321]. The equations and their applications are also described in several survey
articles, among which we mention Friedrich [155] (see also [156]). All these references have been
useful in assembling the material presented here.
    As in the case of other gauge theories like the Yang–Mills theory discussed in §4.2, the
functional and the equations are invariant under the action of a gauge group. Here the structure
group is U.1/, and so the Gauge group G consists of maps from M into U.1/ Š S1 , u 2 G acts on
a pair .'; A/ via

                                 u .'; A/ D .u1 '; u1 du C A/:

One has

                                      @=u A .u1 '/ D u1 @=A '

and

                                            Fu A D FA ;

so that the functional and the equations (including the perturbed ones) remain invariant under the
action of G. For a given spinc structure ePc , Riemannian metric g and imaginary valued selfdual
2-form as pertubation, one considers the space of solutions of (11.2.14), (11.2.15) modulo the
action of G. This space is called the moduli space M.M; e    Pc ; g; / of solutions. One writes the
second Betti number b2 of M as

                                          b2 D bC C b ;

where bC .b / is the dimension of the subspace of H 2 .M; R/ represented by (anti)selfdual 2-
forms. In Seiberg–Witten theory, it is shown that in case bC > 0, the moduli spaces M.M; e  Pc ; g; /
are finite-dimensional, smooth, compact, oriented manifolds, at least for “generic” . The
compactness here comes from the fact that solutions satisfy uniform estimates (Lemma 11.2.3
and estimates for higher derivatives, see e.g. Jost, Peng and Wang [253] for a general presentation)
that imply convergence of subsequences of families of solutions. This is different from the situation
in Donaldson’s theory of (anti)selfdual connections on SU.2/ bundles where no uniform estimates
hold. The most useful case seems to be where the moduli space is zero-dimensional, i.e. where one
has a finite number of solutions. The theorem of Seiberg–Witten says that if bC > 1 and bC  b
is odd, then the number of solutions counted with orientation is independent of the choice of the
Riemannian metric g and the pertubation and depends only on the spinc structure e     Pc on M. Also,
11.3 Dirac-Harmonic Maps                                                                           647


these moduli spaces are nonempty only for finitely many spinc structures. If .M; g/ in addition has
positive scalar curvature, then in fact all Seiberg–Witten invariants vanish (cf. Corollary 11.2.2). On
the other hand, such Seiberg–Witten invariants, i.e. numbers of solutions counted with orientation,
can often be computed from general index theorems, i.e. from topological data alone, and when
these numbers are found to be nonzero, this yields an obstruction for certain compact, oriented,
differentiable 4-manifolds to carry metrics with positive scalar curvature. For results based on such
ideas, see e.g. Le Brun [58]. The Seiberg–Witten theory can be used to prove, to reprove and to
extend many results from Donaldson theory. Kronheimer and Mrowka [281] and Morgan, Szabó
and Taubes [322] used Seiberg–Witten theory to prove the Thom conjecture, stating that smooth
algebraic curves (i.e. compact complex smooth subvarietes of complex dimension one) in CP2
minimize the genus in their homology classes.
    The Seiberg–Witten equations seem to be particulary useful on symplectic 4-manifolds .M; !/.
Using i! as a perturbation and using the limit  ! 0 for the parameter  introduced into the
equations above (see (11.2.16)), Taubes [411, 412] showed that in the limit the zero set of the
solution ' is a collection of pseudoholomorphic curves in the sense of Gromov [180]. Also, the
curvature FA will concentrate along the pseudoholomorphic curves in the limit  ! 0. In this way,
one may identify the invariants defined by Gromov that are very useful in symplectic geometry,
but hard to compute, with the invariants of Seiberg–Witten that can typically be computed from
topological index theorems. For a generalization of the Seiberg–Witten functional with a potential
term of sixth order, see Ding, Jost, Li, Peng and Wang [109].

Perspectives The variational problem presented in this section is a mathematical version of the
nonlinear supersymmetric sigma model of quantum field theory [137, 138, 236]. The mathematical
structure of that model was worked out in detail in [247]. In that model, the variables and fields are
Grassmann instead of real valued. In particular, the ones corresponding to the spinor represent
fermionic particles and are anticommuting. The theory is developed in more generality, including
a systematic geometric treatment of super Riemann surfaces, that is, the domains on which the
action functional is defined, and their deformations, in [271].
    It was discovered in [82] that one still obtains a rich mathematical structure when one makes
all fields real valued, and therefore commuting, even though one then loses the supersymmetry.
The conformal invariance of the functional L, however, is not affected. Here, we have followed
that reference. Further analytic results are derived in [81]. A more general geometric framework
for such action functionals with commuting variables, but also including an additional gravitino
type field is developed in [248].
    For other extensions, see for instance [50–52, 251].
    It remains to explore the geometric significance of Dirac-harmonic maps and their generaliza-
tions further, but since they arise from a deep structure in quantum field theory, one naturally also
expects deep geometric applications. The physical aspects including supersymmetry are discussed
in [137, 138, 236]. The supersymmetric action functional, that is, involving also anticommuting
variables, as in supersymmetric quantum field theory, is systematically investigated in [247].
In [84], the D-branes in superstring theory are converted into a partially free boundary value
problem for Dirac-harmonic maps, and the corresponding boundary regularity theory is developed,
returning to the setting with commuting variables only. Also, a new type of heat flow for Dirac
harmonic maps was introduced in [83] and further studied in [85, 250]. That heat flow consists of
a mixed parabolic-elliptic system; it turns the second order equation (11.3.12) into the parabolic
equations

                             @f .x; t/
                                       D . f .x; t//  R. f .x; t/; .x; t//
                                @t
and carries the first order equation (11.3.13) along as an elliptic constraint.
   In a similar vein as passing from harmonic to Dirac-harmonic maps by coupling the map with
a spinor field, one can also pass from the Liouville equation of conformal geometry to a super-
Liouville system by coupling with a spinor field [256], and this likewise leads to a very interesting
mathematical structure.
   The variational problems presented and analyzed in this chapter, as well as those in earlier
chapters like the Yang–Mills functional, form important links between high energy theoretical
physics and geometry. This perspective is more systematically explored in, for instance, [236, 300].

A.1 Sobolev Spaces

We are going to use the integration theory of Lebesgue. Therefore, we shall always
identify functions which differ only on a set of measure zero. Thus, when we speak
about a function, we actually always mean an equivalence class of functions under
the above identification. In particular, a statement like “the function f is continuous”
is to be interpreted as “f differs from a continuous function at most on a set of
measure zero” or equivalently “the equivalence class of f contains a continuous
function”.
    Replacing functions by their equivalence classes is necessary in order to make
the Lp - and Sobolev spaces Banach spaces.

The restriction to t  t0 > 0 can be avoided if the initial values f0 satisfy appropriate
regularity results. The estimates on Œ0; 1/ will then naturally also involve the
corresponding norms of f0 .
   Theorem A.3.2 concerns a linear parabolic equation. In the text, we shall
encounter nonlinear parabolic equations and systems. For those, the global existence
and regularity cannot be deduced from a general result, but rather needs to invoke
the detailed structure of the system. What one can deduce from Theorem A.3.2,
however, is the short time existence of solutions when the linearization of the
differential operator satisfies the assumptions of that theorem. This follows by
linearization and the implicit function theorem. That means that for such nonlinear
systems, we can obtain the existence of a solution on some interval Œ0; T/ whose
length depends on the regularity properties of the initial values. This also implies
that the maximal interval of existence for nonlinear parabolic systems is open. For
the closedness of the interval of existence, and consequently the existence of a
solution for all “time” t  0, one then needs to derive specific a-priori estimates
that prevent solutions from becoming singular in finite time.
   A reference for parabolic differential equations and systems is [283]. For a
textbook treatment, we refer to [244].
